Meeting header:
Date: 2025-08-14 15:00 UTC
Duration: 62 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam O'Connor (Redwood SE), Sara Patel (Aurelius Platform), Rajiv Menon (Aurelius SecOps), Hannah Lee (Aurelius SRE)

Auto-summary (auto-generated may be noisy) : Deep dive on private vpc, networking edges, runbook, benchmark plan, action items to share docs.

[00:00] Maya: hey everyone thanks for carving out the time, I'm Maya from Redwood, with Liam from our SE team. Quick roll call?
[00:12] Sara: Sara here, platform, hi
[00:15] Rajiv: Rajiv, SecOps
[00:18] Hannah: Hannah, SRE
[00:22] Liam: Liam, SE, thanks all
[00:30] Maya: goal for today is to walk through Private VPC options — PrivateLink, peering, transit gateway — and then dig into runtime tradeoffs, like KV cache persistence, batching, and quantization, and how network design affects latency. We'll capture next steps and run benchmarks.
[00:50] Sara: high level we need to know impact on egress, if PrivateLink introduces lags, also our security team wants KMS and audit logs end-to-end. We also have a multi-account setup with staging and prod separated by account per team.
[01:10] Liam: cool, so start with networking. PrivateLink creates an interface endpoint in your VPC, traffic goes over AWS backbone to Redwood's Private service, so you avoid public internet egress. It's typically lower jitter vs NAT + internet but there is some additional hop to the endpoint ENI. In our experience added latency is small, like single-digit ms for control plane, but depends on AZ placement.
[01:40] Rajiv: when you say single digit, is that p95 or median? our concern is p95/p99 for inference latency.
[01:48] Liam: good call — median is 3-6ms, p95 can be 10-20ms if cross-AZ or if ENI is busy. For token streaming path in high-throughput scenarios we look at end-to-end additional 8-15ms typically versus co-located.
[02:10] Hannah: what about NAT + IGW path if we go with outbound-only (we prefer no internet ingress)? NAT gateway can have burst limits and adds about 5-10ms depending on region as well, and if you have autoscaling NATs you can avoid cold spots but more ops.
[02:30] Maya: yes NAT adds egress hops and cost, PrivateLink is preferred for private connectivity. There's also VPC peering which is L3 but doesn't scale well across many accounts, transit gateway helps with hub-and-spoke. We usually recommend PrivateLink for SaaS endpoints where customers want minimal ops and private DNS via private hosted zones.
[02:55] Sara: ok, how do DNS and split-horizon work? we have internal AWS Route53 private hosted zones and some on-prem DNS forwarders.
[03:05] Liam: we set up private hosted zone with the model endpoints (e.g., api.redwood.private) and then create an A-record to the interface endpoint. For hybrid on-prem we recommend conditional forwarders or Route53 Resolver inbound/outbound endpoints. That way your on-prem resolves the private name to the PrivateLink ENI and traffic never goes over public. There can be TTL considerations and resolution caching, occasionally teams see stale resolutions if they have long TTLs.
[03:40] Rajiv: any gotchas with cross-account PrivateLink? we have a shared network account.
[03:45] Maya: you can subscribe across accounts, you accept the endpoint service and authorize the provider. We can share a step-by-step diagram. Also IAM policy + security groups on the ENI control which subnets can reach it.
[03:58] Hannah: about security groups and NACLs — are there ports to open? we want to minimize blast radius.
[04:04] Liam: mostly HTTPS 443 for API and optionally a tunneling port if using streaming websockets, long-lived connections, but SG rules should be tight — source CIDRs limited to app subnets. NACLs are stateless so ensure ephemeral ports allowed on return. We'll include sample SG/NACL configs.
[04:25] Maya: switching to runtime: Liam, wanna walk KV cache and batching?
[04:29] Liam: sure. Redwood runtime uses a KV cache for prefix and KV cache entries to avoid recomputing attention keys for repeated prefixes — that reduces tokens per second on the model. For Private we support both ephemeral KV cache (in-memory on the GPU host) and a persistent cache option backed by a customer-managed Redis in the VPC if you want warm starts across VM restarts. Ephemeral is fast but lost on pod evict; persistent adds network hops to Redis which can add 1-4ms depending on subnet placement.
[05:05] Sara: persistent Redis in our VPC — are we responsible for HA? and does it need to be in same AZ?
[05:11] Liam: yes for production you'd want multi-AZ replication and colocate in same AZs to minimize cross-AZ latency. For throughput-sensitive workloads we recommend in-AZ Redis or use our local ephemeral cache plus warmup strategies (prefetch).
[05:28] Hannah: how much does the caching affect tail latency?
[05:31] Liam: if cache hit, you can shave 20-40% of token generation time for large contexts because you avoid repeated KV computation. Misses will pay the penalty. So hit rate tuning matters — batch similar prompts, prefix caching, and routing by customer can help.
[05:50] Rajiv: batching — what's the tradeoff for latency vs cost?
[05:53] Liam: batching increases throughput and reduces cost per token but increases per-request latency because you wait to fill a batch or have a batching timeout. We provide adaptive batching where we set a max batch size and a latency cap — for example a 10ms batching wait to assemble micro-batches, or 50ms for more aggressive cost savings. For aurlelius use-case, if you need p95 < 120ms we probably keep batching wait under 20ms and tune max batch to match throughput.
[06:23] Sara: do you support dynamic batch sizing around model variants? we have short queries and some long contexts.
[06:28] Liam: yes, runtime partitions by sequence length and model variant, so long context requests are batched separately. Also you can pin a high-priority route for latency-critical calls to bypass big batch waits.
[06:40] Maya: quantization — impact on latency/throughput and quality?
[06:44] Liam: quantization to INT8 or 4-bit reduces memory and increases throughput on some kernels. INT8 tends to have ~1.2-1.6x throughput improvement and small latency reduction per token; 4-bit can be 1.5-2x but varies by model and the kernel. There's a quality tradeoff; we run a small eval on your prompts to validate. Also some quantized kernels have different kernel selection which may affect latency consistency. We'll include recommended quantization profiles for your models.
[07:20] Hannah: how do quantized models behave with the KV cache? any incompatibility?
[07:25] Liam: KV cache format is compatible across quantization variants only if the runtime supports the same KV layout. If you roll out quantized variant as a different model id, the cache won't be shared. We typically keep quantized variants as fallback or for cost tiers. That said, within a single model variant, quantization doesn't change KV semantics.
[07:50] Sara: and if we do private on-prem — air-gapped — what's different?
[07:55] Maya: on-prem package includes a customer-controlled control plane with a connector, or in full air-gapped mode you run our on-prem agent and we provide an offline installer. Networking is entirely internal; PrivateLink isn't used. You'd handle updates and model pulls via approved artifact storage. We do still recommend internal DNS + service discovery and an internal Redis for cache.
[08:20] Rajiv: audit logs and KMS, HSM — how integrated?
[08:24] Liam: we integrate with customer KMS for model keys and secrets; HSM support for highest compliance is possible with an additional integration. Audit logs can be streamed to your SIEM via Kinesis or forwarders. We'll share the SOC2 packet and example log schema.
[08:42] Maya: ok lets talk benchmarks — what do we need from Aurelius to run a meaningful test?
[08:47] Liam: a traffic profile: qps distribution, seq length histogram (p25/p50/p95), concurrency targets, and a staging subnet with PrivateLink or egress path configured. We'll run 3 profiles: latency-critical (small seq), mixed (mixed context lengths), and throughput (long sequences) and record median/p95/p99 and tokens/sec.
[09:10] Hannah: what's a realistic success criteria? we were thinking 95th <= 120ms for most short queries and ability to sustain 15k tokens/sec for peak.
[09:20] Liam: that seems doable depending on model and hardware. For example for a 8k sequence model on A100-class hardware with INT8 quant we usually see X tokens/sec (we'll put numbers in doc) and p95s around 100-140ms depending on batching. We'll tune the batch window and caching to hit your SLOs.
[09:42] Rajiv: firewall rules — do you have a recommended minimal egress policy?
[09:46] Maya: yes we provide a checklist: allow outbound to PrivateLink ENI CIDRs on 443, allow outbound to Redis cluster endpoints (if persistent cache), and outbound to our metrics collector if you're using it (can be routed via VPC endpoints). We'll send a template.
[10:05] Sara: any notes on cost tradeoffs? PrivateLink has per-hour endpoint costs and data processing charges, NAT has egress data cost also, transit gateway has attachments fees. Dedicated capacity vs hosted — if we want predictable latency we might choose Dedicated reserved pools.
[10:22] Liam: exactly — we'll lay out an example cost math for typical qps to show when Dedicated reserved GPU pools make sense vs hosted with PrivateLink.
[10:30] Maya: quick recap before we move to wrap: action items and owners. We'll send diagrams, benchmarking plan, and security docs.
[10:38] Rajiv: one more question on DNS TTLs — we saw earlier you mentioned stale entries, can you recommend TTLs?
[10:44] Liam: keep TTLs short for PrivateLink endpoints (30-60s) if you plan to move endpoints or in failover scenarios. Longer TTLs ok if stable but then you might have delayed failover. Route53 resolver caching may also affect these.
[10:58] Hannah: for benchmarking can you simulate cold-start cache misses? we want realistic tail numbers.
[11:03] Liam: yes we'll include cold-start scenarios and mixture of warm/cold. We'll also test with persistent Redis vs ephemeral to compare.
[11:15] Maya: ok thanks everyone, we'll share the docs and schedule the benchmark. Any final notes?
[11:22] Sara: thanks this was helpful, look forward to the diagram
[11:24] Rajiv: thanks
[11:25] Hannah: thanks all
[11:27] Maya: end meeting
